Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Male Presence: Being alone with men, Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous, Somatic Pain (Neck): Neck pain
  Maladaptive Strategies: Memory Detachment: I detach myself from the memories, Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Vignette:
Quang was thirty-four when the men took him. They held him in a concrete storage room for twenty-three days, his wrists bound to a steel beam, watching two guards pace the floor. What frightened him most was the constant presence of those men, their heavy boots, the way their shoulders shifted when they leaned in to speak or adjust their belts. When the ropes finally came loose, the pressure marks on his neck remained long after the doors opened. Now sixty-nine, he still carries that familiar tightness in his shoulders and the dull, localized ache of his cervical spine. In the months that followed, he noticed his body responding to the same quiet pressures. A wave of nausea would settle in his stomach, not from illness but from the unspoken weight of being watched, even when no one was there. His wife, Lin, would call him to dinner, but he would often sit at the table alone, eyes fixed on the doorway, certain that any man walking through it might suddenly reach toward him. His recollections of those weeks did not arrive as stories but as fragments that looped without pause. The steel beam, the guards’ breath, the dim fluorescent light—they played over and over in his mind like a film he could not turn off. When Lin or his grandchildren asked him what it had felt like, he would open his mouth to answer, but the words would slip away. He knew exactly what had happened; he could point to the coldness, the pressure, the silence. Yet the language refused to come, and he would lose his thread mid-sentence, leaving the question hanging in the air. Over time, he had come to believe it was easier to step back from the memories altogether, letting them drift behind a quiet glass wall rather than force himself to hold them. He avoided the anniversary dates quietly, slipping out of family gatherings or pretending a prior commitment when the autumn months approached, though he never explained why. As a plumber, Quang spent his days crawling through ductwork and kneeling in homeowners’ basements, but his trade also brought him into repeated contact with the very presence that unsettled him. He worked primarily with male contractors and clients, and when he found himself alone in a basement with a foreman or a homeowner, his pulse would quicken. A sudden shift of a wrench, a man stepping too quickly past him, or even a neighbor’s abrupt wave from the porch would send his body into immediate physical alert. He felt on guard even inside his own house, his posture rigid, his neck aching with a familiar pull. Before entering any new room, he would scan the exits, counting doors, mapping his path back to the street. These were not fears he voiced aloud; they were habits that formed over years, quiet accommodations that shaped his days. For months, he managed, balancing his routines and letting the nausea and neck tension rise and fall with the seasons. But recently, the symptoms stopped waiting for him. The nausea would strike during a site visit when two men argued over a pipe, his neck stiffening until he had to step outside for air. His wife noticed how he would flinch at the sound of a heavy door closing, how he would trace the escape route in his mind before accepting an invitation. It was the constant watching, the unspoken threat in every movement, that finally brought him to the clinic. He does not seek a cure so much as he seeks a space where he can sit without bracing, where the men around him move slowly, and where the memories can play without demanding his attention. What he hopes for is simply a steady quiet, a body at rest, and the certainty that he will be seen, but not captured.
